results.title: Kourovka Problem 17.62 (two-generated characteristic quotients of free groups)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for every natural number $n \ge 3$ the free group $F_n$ on $n$ generators has a characteristic subgroup $C \ne F_n$ such that the quotient $F_n / C$ is generated by two elements, hence by fewer than $n$ elements. This is the positive answer to Problem 17.62 (J. Conrad) in every rank where two generators are fewer than $n$.

results.title: Free groups of rank at least 3 have proper two-generated characteristic quotients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n \ge 3$, the free group $F_n$ on $n$ generators has a characteristic subgroup $C \ne F_n$ such that the quotient $F_n / C$ is generated by two elements; since $2 < n$, the quotient is generated by fewer than $n$ elements.

results.title: Congruence subgroup
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathfrak m$ a modulus of $K$. A congruence subgroup for $\mathfrak m$ is a subgroup $H$ of the group of invertible fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$ such that $H$ contains the ray group of $\mathfrak m$.

results.title: Image of a congruence subgroup in the ray class group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $H$ be a congruence subgroup for a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of a number field $K$, and let $\pi$ be the canonical projection from the group of invertible fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$ onto the ray class group of $\mathfrak m$. The image of $H$ is the subgroup $\pi(H)$ of the ray class group.

results.title: Membership in the image of a congruence subgroup
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a congruence subgroup for a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of a number field $K$, and let $\pi$ be the canonical projection from the group of invertible fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$ onto the ray class group of $\mathfrak m$. An element $x$ of the ray class group lies in the image $\pi(H)$ if and only if $\pi(y) = x$ for some $y \in H$.

results.title: Congruence subgroup as a subgroup of all invertible fractional ideals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a congruence subgroup $H$ for a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of a number field $K$, this is the image of $H$ under the inclusion of the group of invertible fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$ into the group of all invertible fractional ideals of $K$.

results.title: Smallest congruence subgroup
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of a number field $K$, the smallest congruence subgroup for $\mathfrak m$ is the ray group of $\mathfrak m$ itself, a subgroup of the group of invertible fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$.

results.title: Largest congruence subgroup
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of a number field $K$, the largest congruence subgroup for $\mathfrak m$ is the whole group of invertible fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$, which contains the ray group of $\mathfrak m$.

results.title: Congruence subgroup pair
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field. A congruence subgroup pair for $K$ consists of a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of $K$ together with a congruence subgroup for $\mathfrak m$, that is, a subgroup of the group of invertible fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$ that contains the ray group of $\mathfrak m$.

results.title: Equivalence of congruence subgroup pairs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field. For a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of $K$, write $I^{\mathfrak m}$ for the group of nonzero fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$. Two pairs $(\mathfrak m, H)$ and $(\mathfrak n, H')$, each consisting of a modulus of $K$ and a congruence subgroup for it, are equivalent when $I^{\mathfrak m} \cap H' = I^{\mathfrak n} \cap H$, where both congruence subgroups are…

results.title: Criterion for equivalence of congruence subgroup pairs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field, and for a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of $K$ write $I^{\mathfrak m}$ for the group of nonzero fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$. Two pairs $(\mathfrak m, H)$ and $(\mathfrak n, H')$, each consisting of a modulus of $K$ and a congruence subgroup for it, are equivalent if and only if $I^{\mathfrak m} \cap H' = I^{\mathfrak n} \cap H$ in the group of all nonzero…

results.title: Equivalence of congruence subgroup pairs is reflexive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field. Every pair consisting of a modulus of $K$ and a congruence subgroup for it is equivalent to itself.

results.title: Equivalence of congruence subgroup pairs is symmetric
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field. If a pair $P$, consisting of a modulus of $K$ and a congruence subgroup for it, is equivalent to such a pair $Q$, then $Q$ is equivalent to $P$.

results.title: Ray group among all fractional ideals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of a number field $K$, the ambient ray group of $\mathfrak m$ is the image of the ray group of $\mathfrak m$ under the inclusion of the group of nonzero fractional ideals of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$ into the group of all nonzero fractional ideals of $K$.

results.title: The ray group consists of coprime ideals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every modulus $\mathfrak m$ of a number field $K$, the ray group of $\mathfrak m$, viewed as a subgroup of the group of nonzero fractional ideals of $K$, is contained in the group of nonzero fractional ideals coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m$.

results.title: A congruence subgroup contains the ray group
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C$ be a congruence subgroup for a modulus $\mathfrak m$ of a number field $K$. Viewed as subgroups of the group of nonzero fractional ideals of $K$, the ray group of $\mathfrak m$ is contained in $C$.

results.title: Coprimality passes to divisors of a modulus
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mathfrak m_1$ and $\mathfrak m_2$ be moduli of a number field $K$ with $\mathfrak m_2 \mid \mathfrak m_1$. Then every nonzero fractional ideal of $K$ coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m_1$ is coprime to the finite part of $\mathfrak m_2$.

Viewed as subgroups of the group of nonzero fractional ideals of $K$, the change of modulus of $C_1$ to $\mathfrak m_2$ equals the subgroup generated by $C_1$ and the ray group $P_{\mathfrak m_2}$ of $\mathfrak m_2$.

results.title: Admissible sequences for Taylor's law
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A sequence $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, indexed from $1$ (its value at $0$ is ignored), is admissible when $a(n) > 0$ for every $n \ge 1$ and there is $n_0 \ge 1$ such that $a(n) < a(n + 1)$ for every $n \ge n_0$.

results.title: Initial-segment mean
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a sequence $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the initial-segment mean is the real number $m(a, n) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a(j)$, with the convention $1 / 0 = 0$, so that $m(a, 0) = 0$.

results.title: Initial-segment sample variance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a sequence $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the unbiased initial-segment sample variance is the real number $v(a, n) = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \left(a(j) - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a(k)\right)^2$, with the convention $1 / 0 = 0$; in particular $v(a, 0) = v(a, 1) = 0$.

results.title: Taylor's law, asymptotic form
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A sequence $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, indexed from $1$ (its value at $0$ is ignored), satisfies Taylor's law asymptotically when it is admissible for Taylor's law and, writing $m(a, n)$ and $v(a, n)$ for its initial-segment mean and initial-segment sample variance, there are real numbers $c > 0$ and $b$ such that $v(a, n) / m(a, n)^b \to c$ as $n \to \infty$.

results.title: Von Neumann measures on a complete Boolean algebra
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real-valued function $\mu$ on a complete Boolean algebra $B$ is a measure in von Neumann's sense when $\mu(\bot) = 0$, $\mu(a) > 0$ for every $a \ne \bot$, and $\mu$ is countably additive: for every sequence $(a_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of pairwise disjoint elements of $B$ (that is, $a_i \wedge a_j = \bot$ whenever $i \ne j$), the series $\sum_i \mu(a_i)$ converges and $\mu(\bigvee_i a_i) = \sum_i \mu(a_i)$.

results.title: The countable chain condition for complete Boolean algebras
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A complete Boolean algebra $B$ satisfies the countable chain condition (von Neumann's condition (5)) when every subset $S \subseteq B$ whose distinct elements are pairwise disjoint (that is, $a \wedge b = \bot$ for all distinct $a, b \in S$) is at most countable.

results.title: Von Neumann's generalized distributivity law
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A complete Boolean algebra $B$ satisfies the generalized distributivity law (von Neumann's condition (6)) when, for every double sequence $(a_{i,j})_{i, j \in \mathbb{N}}$ of elements of $B$ that is increasing in $j$ for each fixed $i$ (that is, $a_{i,0} \le a_{i,1} \le \cdots$ for every $i$),

results.title: Von Neumann's sufficiency claim
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that every complete Boolean algebra satisfying the countable chain condition and the generalized distributivity law carries a measure in von Neumann's sense.

results.title: Von Neumann's conditions do not guarantee a measure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a complete Boolean algebra that satisfies the countable chain condition and the generalized distributivity law but carries no measure in von Neumann's sense; that is, von Neumann's sufficiency claim is false. This answers Problem 163 of the Scottish Book in the negative, in its stated form.

results.title: Square word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A word $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a square if $w = xx$ for some nonempty word $x$, where $xx$ denotes the concatenation of $x$ with itself.

results.title: Square-free finite word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A finite word $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is square-free if no factor of $w$ is a square, where a factor of $w$ is a word $s$ with $w = psq$ for some words $p$ and $q$, and a square is a word $xx$ with $x$ nonempty.

results.title: Square-free infinite word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is square-free if it contains no two adjacent equal nonempty blocks: for all $i \ge 0$ and all $k \ge 1$ there is some $j < k$ with $u_{i+j} \ne u_{i+k+j}$.

results.title: The ternary alphabet for square-free words
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The ternary alphabet is the set $\{0, 1, 2\}$ of natural numbers less than $3$; its three letters play the role of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

results.title: Square-free ternary words of length $n$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, a finite word $w$ over the ternary alphabet is a square-free ternary word of length $n$ if $w$ is square-free and $w$ has length exactly $n$.

results.title: Square-free infinite ternary word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over the ternary alphabet is a square-free infinite ternary word if it is square-free as an infinite word.

results.title: Factors of square-free words are square-free
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a finite word $v$ is square-free and $u$ is a factor of $v$, that is, $v = puq$ for some words $p$ and $q$, then $u$ is square-free.

results.title: Square-freeness via prefixes of suffixes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A finite word $w$ is square-free if and only if, for every prefix $s$ of a suffix of $w$ and every nonempty prefix $x$ of $s$, we have $s \ne xx$, where $xx$ denotes the concatenation of $x$ with itself.

results.title: Crochemore's square-freeness test
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ map each letter of the three-letter alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$ to a finite word over a set $T$, and extend $f$ to words by concatenation, $f(x_1 \cdots x_n) = f(x_1) \cdots f(x_n)$. Then $f$ maps every square-free word over $\{a, b, c\}$ to a square-free word if and only if it maps every square-free word over $\{a, b, c\}$ of length at most $5$ to a square-free word.

results.title: Weighted tardy jobs instances
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of WEIGHTED NUMBER OF TARDY JOBS is a pair consisting of a finite list of jobs, each a triple $(p, d, w)$ of natural numbers giving its processing time $p$, due date $d$ and weight $w$, and a natural number $K$, the bound.

results.title: One step of the weighted tardy jobs computation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $J$ be a list of jobs, each a triple $(p, d, w)$ of natural numbers (processing time, due date, weight). Given a state $(t, s)$ and a natural number $j$, let $(p, d, w)$ be the job at position $j$ of $J$, counting from $0$, or $(0, 0, 0)$ if $J$ has no position $j$, and let $t' = t + p$. The step returns $(t', s + w)$ if $d < t'$, and $(t', s)$ otherwise.

results.title: Weighted number of tardy jobs of an ordering
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $J$ be a list of jobs, each a triple of natural numbers (processing time, due date, weight), and write $(p_i, d_i, w_i)$ for the job at position $i$ of $J$, counting from $0$, with $(p_i, d_i, w_i) = (0, 0, 0)$ when $J$ has no position $i$. For a list $(j_1, \dots, j_m)$ of natural numbers, the weighted number of tardy jobs of this order is the sum of $w_{j_k}$ over all $k$ with $d_{j_k} < C_k$, where…

results.title: Feasible weighted tardy jobs instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A weighted tardy jobs instance, consisting of a list of $n$ jobs and a bound $K$, is feasible when there is an ordering of its jobs, that is, a list of the job indices $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ in which each index occurs exactly once, whose weighted number of tardy jobs is at most $K$.

results.title: The weighted number of tardy jobs decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: WEIGHTED NUMBER OF TARDY JOBS is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of weighted tardy jobs instances, to a feasible instance, that is, an instance having an ordering of its jobs whose weighted number of tardy jobs is at most its bound. A bitstring that decodes to no instance is rejected.

results.title: WEIGHTED NUMBER OF TARDY JOBS is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The weighted number of tardy jobs decision problem lies in NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

results.title: Minesweeper instances
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A Minesweeper instance consists of a number of rows $R$, a number of columns $C$ and a finite list of clues, where $R$ and $C$ are natural numbers and each clue is a triple $(r, c, k)$ of natural numbers giving a row $r$, a column $c$ and the number $k$ shown.

results.title: Well-formed Minesweeper instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A Minesweeper instance with $R$ rows, $C$ columns and a list of clues is well formed when every clue $(r, c, k)$ in the list satisfies $r < R$, $c < C$ and $k \le 8$.

results.title: Feasible Minesweeper instances

results.title: Minesweeper consistency as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Minesweeper consistency decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a Minesweeper instance that is well formed and feasible, that is, admits a mine placement consistent with all of its clues. It rejects every bitstring that does not decode to a Minesweeper instance.

results.title: Regular-expression node
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A node of an encoded regular expression over an alphabet $\alpha$ is one of six kinds: zero, epsilon, a letter $a \in \alpha$, a sum with arguments $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, a product (concatenation) with arguments $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, or a star with argument $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where the arguments are indices of nodes.

results.title: Encoded regular expressions
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An encoded regular expression over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a list of regular-expression nodes, each a constant ($0$, $1$ or a letter) or an operator (sum, concatenation or star) whose arguments are node indices; the last node is the root. Any list is allowed: in the semantics, an argument that is not the index of an earlier node reads as $0$, and the empty list denotes $0$.

results.title: Node at an index
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and a natural number $k$, the node of $e$ at index $k$ is the entry at position $k$ (counting from $0$) of its list of nodes, or the zero node when $k$ is at least the length of the list.

results.title: Regular expression at a node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the regular expression at node $k$ is defined by recursion on $k$ from the node of $e$ at index $k$ (a zero node when $k$ is past the end): a zero node gives $0$, an epsilon node gives $1$, a node for a letter $a$ gives $a$, and a sum, product or star node gives the sum, product or star of the regular expressions at its arguments, where an argument that…

results.title: The regular expression denoted by an encoding
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An encoded regular expression $e$ with $n$ nodes denotes the regular expression at its node $n - 1$, the last node. For $n = 0$ this is the expression at node $0$, which lies past the end of the list and is the empty expression $0$.

results.title: Appending nodes does not change earlier expressions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $l$ and $m$ be lists of regular-expression nodes and let $k$ be smaller than the length of $l$. Then the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$ followed by $m$ equals the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$.

results.title: Postorder encoding after a prefix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a regular expression $r$ and a list $l$ of nodes, the nodes of $r$ are appended after $l$ in postorder, by recursion on $r$. For $0$, $1$ and a letter $a$, append the single node $0$, $1$ or $a$. For a sum $s + t$ (respectively a concatenation $st$), append the nodes of $s$ after $l$, giving $l_1$, then the nodes of $t$ after $l_1$, giving $l_2$, then a sum (respectively concatenation) node with arguments…

results.title: Encoding of a regular expression
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The encoding of a regular expression $r$ is the list of nodes obtained by appending the nodes of $r$ in postorder after the empty list, so that the root of $r$ is the last node.

results.title: Every regular expression has an encoding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every regular expression $r$ over an alphabet $\alpha$, the encoded regular expression obtained by flattening $r$ (listing the nodes of its subexpressions in postorder, so that the root of $r$ is the last node) denotes $r$.

results.title: Flags of the empty language
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The flag triple of the empty language is $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$; the three flags of a language say whether it is nonempty, whether it has a nonempty word, and whether it is infinite. This triple is also read for an argument of a node that is not an earlier node.

results.title: Flags of a sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For triples of booleans $b = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ and $c = (c_1, c_2, c_3)$, the flags of the sum are $(b_1 \lor c_1, b_2 \lor c_2, b_3 \lor c_3)$.

results.title: Flags of a concatenation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For triples of Booleans $b = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ and $c = (c_1, c_2, c_3)$, the flags of the product are $(b_1 \land c_1,\ (b_2 \land c_1) \lor (b_1 \land c_2),\ (b_3 \land c_1) \lor (b_1 \land c_3))$.

results.title: Flags of a star
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a triple of Booleans $(b_1, b_2, b_3)$, the flags of its star are $(\mathrm{true}, b_2, b_2)$. Read as the flags (nonempty, has a nonempty word, infinite) of a language, a star is always nonempty, and it has a nonempty word, and is infinite, exactly when the argument has a nonempty word.

results.title: Flags of the next node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given the list $A$ of flag triples of the nodes before it, the flag triple of a node is $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ for a zero node, $(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ for an epsilon node and $(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false})$ for a letter node. For a sum, product or star node it is the flags of a sum, product or star applied to the entries of $A$ at its…

results.title: Flags of all nodes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list of nodes $n_0, \dots, n_{m-1}$, the flags $f_0, \dots, f_{m-1}$ are computed in one left-to-right pass: $f_k$ is the step flags of node $n_k$ computed from the flags $f_0, \dots, f_{k-1}$ of the nodes before it.

results.title: Flags of a language
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A triple of Booleans $(b_1, b_2, b_3)$ describes a language $L$ when $b_1$ is true exactly when $L$ is nonempty, $b_2$ is true exactly when $L$ contains a nonempty word, and $b_3$ is true exactly when $L$ is infinite.

results.title: Correctness of the flag pass
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a list $l$ of nodes and a natural number $k$, let $f_k$ be the entry at position $k$ of the flags of $l$, or the zero flags $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ if $k$ is at least the length of $l$. Then $f_k$ describes the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding $l$ when $k$ is less than the length of $l$, and describes the empty language otherwise.

results.title: Infiniteness test for encoded regular expressions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $e$ be an encoded regular expression with nodes $n_0, \dots, n_{m-1}$, and let $f_0, \dots, f_{m-1}$ be the flags of all nodes of $e$, the triples of Booleans computed in one left-to-right pass over the nodes. The infiniteness test of $e$ is the third component of $f_{m-1}$, the flag triple of the last node (the root); when $e$ has no nodes it is false.

results.title: Productions of a sum node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $k$, $i$ and $j$, the productions of a sum node $k$ with arguments $i$ and $j$ are the unit production $k \to i$ if $i < k$, followed by the unit production $k \to j$ if $j < k$ (and nothing else). Nonterminals are node indices.

results.title: Productions of a concatenation node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $k$, $i$ and $j$, the productions of a concatenation node $k$ with arguments $i$ and $j$ are the single production $k \to i\,j$ (nonterminal $i$ followed by nonterminal $j$) when $i < k$ and $j < k$, and there are none otherwise.

results.title: Productions of a star node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the productions of a star node $k$ with argument $i$ are $k \to \varepsilon$, followed by $k \to i\,k$ if $i < k$ (and nothing else). Nonterminals are node indices.

results.title: Productions of a node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $k$ and a node $n$, the productions of node $k$ are the following encoded productions, all with left-hand side $k$, where nonterminal $i$ stands for node $i$: none if $n$ is the zero node; $k \to \varepsilon$ if $n$ is the empty-word node; $k \to a$ if $n$ is the character $a$; if $n$ is a sum with arguments $i$ and $j$, the unit production $k \to i$ when $i < k$ and the unit production…

results.title: The grammar of an encoded regular expression
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ with $n$ nodes, its grammar is the encoded context-free grammar with start nonterminal $n - 1$ (truncated subtraction, so $0$ when $n = 0$), in which nonterminal $k$ stands for node $k$. Its productions are, for each node $k < n$: none if node $k$ is $0$; $k \to \varepsilon$ if it is $\varepsilon$; if it is the letter $a$, the production $k \to a$; if it is the sum of nodes $i$…

results.title: Language of a sentential form
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$, the language of a sentential form $X_1 \cdots X_n$ (terminals in $\alpha$, nonterminals in $\mathbb{N}$) is the product $L_1 \cdots L_n$, where $L_i$ is $\{a\}$, the language of the one-letter word $a$, when $X_i$ is the terminal $a$, and the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of $e$ when $X_i$ is the nonterminal $k$. The empty form has language $\{\varepsilon\}$.

results.title: A production of a node only produces words of its language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e$ be an encoded regular expression, $k$ a natural number and $x$ one of the productions of node $k$ built from the node of $e$ at index $k$. If a word $w$ belongs to the language of the right-hand side of $x$ (the concatenation, over its symbols, of $\{a\}$ for a terminal $a$ and of the language of the regular expression at node $i$ for a nonterminal $i$), then $w$ belongs to the language of the regular…

results.title: Soundness of the grammar of a regular expression
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e$ be an encoded regular expression. If a sentential form $u$ of the context-free grammar of $e$ yields a terminal word $w$, then $w$ belongs to the language of $u$: the concatenation, over the symbols of $u$, of $\{a\}$ for a terminal $a$ and of the language of the regular expression at node $k$ for a nonterminal $k$.

results.title: Completeness of the grammar of an encoded regular expression
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with decidable equality, $e$ an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ and $k$ a natural number. Every word in the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of $e$ is yielded by the sentential form consisting of the single nonterminal $k$ in the context-free grammar of $e$.

results.title: The grammar generates the language of the expression
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every encoded regular expression $e$, the language of the context-free grammar of $e$ (one nonterminal per node, the root as start symbol) equals the language of the regular expression that $e$ denotes.

results.title: Membership test for regular expressions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and a word $w$, the test returns the answer of the membership test for encoded context-free grammars on the word $w$ and the grammar of $e$, which has one nonterminal per node and the root as start symbol.

results.title: Emptiness test for regular expressions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$, the test returns the answer of the emptiness test for encoded context-free grammars on the grammar of $e$, which has one nonterminal per node and the root as start symbol.

results.title: Inclusion test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and an encoded DFA $D$, the inclusion test returns the Boolean computed by the CFG ⊆ DFA inclusion test on the grammar of $e$ and the automaton $D$.

results.title: Regex nodes as a sum type
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The bijection between the nodes of encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$ and $1 \oplus 1 \oplus \alpha \oplus (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}) \oplus (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}) \oplus \mathbb{N}$, where $1$ is the one-point type, that sends the zero node and the empty-word node to the first and second copies of $1$, a character node $a$ to $a$, a sum node with arguments $i, j$ to $(i, j)$ in the first copy of…

results.title: Encodings are lists of nodes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The map sending an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ to its list of nodes is a bijection onto the lists of regular-expression nodes over $\alpha$; its inverse wraps a list of nodes as an encoding.

results.title: Membership for regular expressions is decidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive coding by natural numbers. The set of pairs $(e, w)$ of an encoded regular expression $e$ over $\alpha$ and a word $w$ over $\alpha$ such that $w$ belongs to the language of the regular expression denoted by $e$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.

results.title: Emptiness of regular expressions is decidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ that the language it denotes is empty (E_REX) is decidable by a multi-stack machine.

results.title: Infiniteness of regular expressions is decidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ that the language it denotes is infinite is decidable by a multi-stack machine.

results.title: Inclusion of a regular language in a DFA language is decidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with decidable equality and a primitive recursive coding by natural numbers. The set of pairs $(e, D)$ of an encoded regular expression $e$ over $\alpha$ and an encoded DFA $D$ over $\alpha$ such that the language of the regular expression denoted by $e$ is contained in the language of $D$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.

results.title: Short distinguishing words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Two regular expressions $r$ and $s$ denote the same language if and only if every word of length less than $2^{n(r) + n(s)}$, where $n$ denotes the Thompson state count, is matched by $r$ exactly when it is matched by $s$.

results.title: One step of the Thompson state count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $c = (c_0, \dots, c_{m-1})$ be a list of natural numbers, and read $c_i$ as $0$ when $i \ge m$. The Thompson state count of a regular-expression node from $c$ is $0$ for the node $0$, $1$ for the node $\varepsilon$, $2$ for a letter, $c_i + c_j$ for a sum node and for a concatenation node with arguments $i$ and $j$, and $c_i + 1$ for a star node with argument $i$.

results.title: Thompson state counts of a node list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $l$ of regular-expression nodes, the list of Thompson state counts of $l$ is computed in one left-to-right pass: starting from the empty list, each node $n$ of $l$ in turn appends the count of $n$ computed from the list of counts built so far.

results.title: Thompson state count of an encoding
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of Thompson states of an encoded regular expression $e$ is the entry of the state counts of the nodes of $e$ at the last node, the root (read as $0$ when $e$ has no nodes).

results.title: One state count per node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $l$ of nodes of encoded regular expressions, the list of state counts of $l$ has the same length as $l$.

results.title: Appending a node appends its count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $l$ of regular-expression nodes and every node $n$, let $l'$ be the list $l$ with $n$ appended at the end. Then the list of Thompson state counts of $l'$ is the list of counts of $l$ followed by one more entry, the count of $n$ computed from the counts of $l$.

results.title: The pass computes the Thompson state count of every node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $l$ of nodes and every index $k$, the entry at index $k$ of the state counts of $l$ (read as $0$ past the end of the list) equals the Thompson state count of the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$ when $k$ is less than the length of $l$, and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: The pass counts the states of Thompson's automaton
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every encoded regular expression $e$, the number of Thompson states of $e$ computed by the pass over its nodes equals the Thompson state count of the regular expression that $e$ denotes.

results.title: Search bound for equivalence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$, the search bound is $2^{m + n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are the numbers of Thompson states of $e_1$ and $e_2$, each computed by one pass over the nodes of the encoding.

results.title: Short distinguishing words for encoded regular expressions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e_1$ and $e_2$ be encoded regular expressions over an alphabet $\alpha$, and let $B$ be their search bound for equivalence. The regular expressions denoted by $e_1$ and $e_2$ match the same language if and only if every word $w$ over $\alpha$ of length less than $B$ is matched by the expression denoted by $e_1$ exactly when it is matched by the expression denoted by $e_2$.

results.title: Equivalence test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Over a finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, the equivalence test of two encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$ returns true exactly when, for every length $n$ less than the search bound of $e_1$ and $e_2$ and every word $w$ of length $n$, the membership test gives the same answer for $e_1$ on $w$ as for $e_2$ on $w$.

results.title: The equivalence test is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Over a finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, for all encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$, the equivalence test returns true on $e_1$ and $e_2$ if and only if the regular expressions that $e_1$ and $e_2$ denote have the same language.

results.title: One step of the Thompson state count is primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the map sending a list $c$ of natural numbers and a regular-expression node over $\alpha$ to the Thompson state count of the node computed from $c$ is primitive recursive.

results.title: The pass of Thompson state counts is primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the map sending a list of regular-expression nodes over $\alpha$ to the list of their Thompson state counts, computed in one left-to-right pass, is primitive recursive.

results.title: The Thompson state count of an encoding is primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the number of states of Thompson's automaton of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$, computed by one pass over its nodes, is a primitive recursive function of the encoding.

results.title: The equivalence search bound is primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the search bound $2^{m+n}$ for equivalence of two encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$, where $m$ and $n$ are the numbers of states of Thompson's automata of the two expressions, is a primitive recursive function of the pair of encoded expressions.

results.title: The equivalence test is primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Over a primitively encodable finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, the equivalence test, as a function of two encoded regular expressions, is primitive recursive.

results.title: EQ_REX is decidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding. Then equivalence of encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine: some multi-stack machine decides, for a pair $(e_1, e_2)$ of encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$, whether the regular expressions that $e_1$ and $e_2$ denote have the same language.

results.title: Karatsuba multiplication
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Karatsuba's algorithm on natural numbers $x$ and $y$, viewed as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$, as a computation that returns a natural number together with a cost. If $n \le 1$, it returns $xy$ at cost $1$. If $n \ge 2$, let $m = \lceil n/2 \rceil$, let $a$ and $b$ be the natural-number quotient and remainder of $x$ by $B^m$, and let $c$ and $d$ be those of $y$ by $B^m$. It runs itself with digit count $m$ on the…

results.title: Karatsuba cost recurrence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The function $T$ on natural numbers defined by $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$.

results.title: Karatsuba's middle coefficient
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $a, b, c, d$, write $P = |a - b| \cdot |c - d|$. If $b \le a$ holds exactly when $d \le c$, then $ac + bd - P = ad + bc$, where the subtraction is truncated at $0$; otherwise $ac + bd + P = ad + bc$.

results.title: Correctness of Karatsuba multiplication
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $B$, $n$, $x$ and $y$, Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$ returns $xy$.

results.title: Size bound for Karatsuba's recursive operands
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $B \ge 1$ and $n$ be natural numbers, let $m = \lceil n/2 \rceil$, and let $x < B^n$ be a natural number. Then the high part $\lfloor x / B^m \rfloor$, the low part $x \bmod B^m$, and their distance $|\lfloor x / B^m \rfloor - x \bmod B^m|$ are all less than $B^m$.

results.title: Cost of Karatsuba multiplication
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $B$, $n$, $x$ and $y$, the cost of Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$ equals $T(n)$, where $T$ is the Karatsuba cost recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$.

results.title: Karatsuba cost at powers of two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be the Karatsuba cost recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$. For every natural number $k$, $T(2^k) + 2^{k+1} = 3^{k+1}$.

results.title: Power-of-three bound on the Karatsuba cost recurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be the Karatsuba cost recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$, and let $\ell(n)$ be the least natural number $k$ with $n \le 2^k$ (so $\ell(n) = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for $n \ge 1$). For every natural number $n$, $T(n) \le 3^{\ell(n) + 1}$.

results.title: Power-of-three bound on the cost of Karatsuba multiplication
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\ell(n)$ be the least natural number $k$ with $n \le 2^k$ (so $\ell(n) = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for $n \ge 1$). For all natural numbers $B$, $n$, $x$ and $y$, the cost of Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$ is at most $3^{\ell(n) + 1}$.

results.title: The $n^{\log_2 3}$ bound for the Karatsuba cost recurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be the Karatsuba cost recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$, $T(n) \le 9\, n^{\log_2 3}$.

results.title: The $n^{\log_2 3}$ bound for Karatsuba multiplication
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $B$, $x$, $y$ and $n \ge 1$, the cost of Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$ is at most $9\, n^{\log_2 3}$.
